component.name: Apache Hadoop
component.description: Distributed storage (HDFS) and compute (YARN, MapReduce) platform. The security model defends a Kerberos-secured cluster running on a trusted operating system, behind a network perimeter, with a valid site configuration; the boundary Hadoop defends is privilege escalation across an authenticated boundary within such a cluster. Findings that only apply outside that model are bugs, not vulnerabilities.

externalReferences.comment: Source security model document (SECURITY.md); this file is a structured translation of it.

blueprints.name: Kerberos-secured Hadoop cluster
blueprints.description: The deployment the security model defends: Kerberos authentication, service-level authorization, delegation tokens, and constrained proxy/superuser impersonation, behind a network perimeter that keeps the public internet out (Hadoop clusters are never web-facing). Variants covered by the model: standalone insecure mode (insecure by design, test only), transient cloud deployments (VM/container-supplied credentials are the trust boundary), and client-only deployments.

assets.name: HDFS (NameNode, DataNodes)
assets.description: Uses Kerberos to authenticate HDFS nodes, other cluster services, and callers; the NameNode issues block tokens granting authenticated principals access to data blocks on DataNodes without further authentication.

assets.name: YARN and MapReduce
assets.description: Executes submitted jobs as the submitter's identity; distributes and renews delegation tokens on an application's behalf so tasks can authenticate to services without holding Kerberos credentials.

assets.name: IPC endpoints
assets.description: Hadoop RPC (Writable + protobuf, not Java serialization) used by Hadoop and applications on it. In a secure cluster they support Kerberos authentication/authorization and may support delegation tokens; access is restricted to callers by ACL site configuration. Not exposed to the internet, so full public-facing DoS resilience is not required.

assets.name: Delegation and block tokens
assets.description: Tokens issued by services (HDFS, HBase, Hive, Knox, ...) with limited lifespan, cancellation, and renewal. Hadoop and applications must safely marshall and store them; publishing them in any form leaks permissions. TokenIdentifier implementations are unmarshalled before callers are authenticated and must resist malicious clients.

assets.name: Site configuration and keytabs
assets.description: core-site.xml, hdfs-site.xml, yarn-site.xml, everything in /etc/hadoop/conf, and Kerberos keytab files: expected to be valid, writable only by trusted administrators, and protected by OS file permissions.

assets.name: Hadoop client libraries
assets.description: hadoop-client-api/-runtime and friends: shaded, relocated aggregates for client-side use. CVEs a scanner reports in them are almost always against a shaded third-party artifact; server-side vulnerabilities in bundled dependencies are not direct issues for the client libraries.

zones.name: Public internet
zones.description: Untrusted. Hadoop clusters are never web-facing; network rules keep the cluster off the public internet. The perimeter does not authenticate callers, Kerberos does that at the service level.

zones.name: Authenticated principals
zones.description: Users and client applications inside the perimeter holding Kerberos credentials or delegation tokens; authenticated but not necessarily authorized for every operation.

zones.name: Cluster services
zones.description: HDFS, YARN, and other cluster services with keytab credentials, enforcing service-level authorization and constrained impersonation.

zones.name: Trusted infrastructure
zones.description: Trusted elements whose compromise is out of scope: cluster administrators, DNS, the Kerberos KDC, the hosting cloud/hardware, the operating system, the site configuration, and the classpath.

assumptions.description: Cluster administrators, DNS, and the Kerberos authentication infrastructure (KDC, with synchronized clocks) are trusted; authentication failures from clock drift are operational bugs.

The network perimeter keeps the public internet out, but the wire is not assumed confidential; wire encryption (RPC privacy QOP, HDFS block-transfer encryption) is optional and controlled by site configuration.

The hosting cloud/infrastructure provider, the hardware (even shared multi-tenant hardware), and the operating system are trusted; hypervisor escape and cross-tenant side channels (speculative execution, Rowhammer) are the provider's responsibility.
The site configuration is valid and writable only by trusted administrators, and the classpath contains no malicious JARs; attacks requiring either are out of scope.

In transient cloud deployments, the cloud credentials supplied by the hosting infrastructure (e.g. IAM roles) are the trust boundary, and network rules must isolate the cluster from the public internet.

In client-only deployments, the OS, principal, host administrator, application classpath, and client-side configuration/CLI arguments are trusted; network trust (DNS, mandatory wire encryption) is a matter of client configuration and out of scope.
Logs are expected to be kept private, with access restricted so non-administrator principals cannot read other principals' application logs or service logs.
Development and CI are explicitly in scope: the compiler, release docker images, build tools, and other ASF projects are trusted, while all inputs from external pull requests are untrusted.

threats.name: A user acting as another user, a service, or a superuser without authorization
threats.description: The core in-scope issue: privilege escalation across an authenticated boundary within a Kerberos-secured cluster, including defeating the constraints on proxy/superuser impersonation.

threats.name: Bypassing service-level authorization or ACLs
threats.description: In a secure cluster, access to service endpoints is restricted to callers by ACL site configuration; bypassing service-level authorization or these ACLs is in scope. For YARN-launched application services, authentication should be restricted to the submitting principal.

threats.name: Forging, leaking, or improperly reusing delegation tokens
threats.description: Delegation tokens have limited lifespans, must be rejected once cancelled, and must be safely marshalled and stored; forging, leaking, or improper reuse is in scope. Any exposure of a secret or delegated credential to a new audience is a higher-confidence finding.

threats.name: Denial of service or authentication bypass via TokenIdentifier unmarshalling
threats.description: Hadoop tokens authenticate IPC channels and are unmarshalled (via Writable) before callers are authenticated; TokenIdentifier implementations in production code must be resilient so malicious clients can neither mount denial-of-service attacks nor bypass or spoof authentication. (For any Writable-related CVE, a submitter must show a valid exploit chain with extant gadgets; implementing new Writable classes as part of an exploit does not count.)

threats.name: Client failure to detect and reject malicious service endpoints or MITM
threats.description: Failure of clients to detect and reject malicious service endpoints or MITM attacks is in scope; TLS certificate validation, including hostname and full-chain verification, is in scope (certificate management is not). If a malicious remote service can trigger RCE on a client, that is a CVE; mere lack of resilience to malformed responses is a bug.

threats.name: Failure of enabled wire or at-rest encryption to protect data
threats.description: Running without encryption is by design and not a vulnerability, but when wire encryption is enabled, a failure to actually protect traffic (no-op encryption, silent downgrade, MITM bypass) is in scope; likewise, where HDFS transparent encryption has been configured, a failure of the code to actually encrypt persisted data is a vulnerability.

threats.name: Non-atomic temporary file creation windows
threats.description: Temporary data goes to local-filesystem temp directories secured by the trusted OS, but code creating temp files and directories must create them and set their permissions atomically; creating with permissive defaults and narrowing later leaves a window in which another local principal can act on the file. Such failures are issues and should be reported.

threats.name: Secrets inserted into logs
threats.description: CWE-532: persistent secrets, long-lived credentials, and encryption secrets must never be logged at any level; transient secrets (short-lived tokens) must not be logged at INFO/WARN/ERROR and should not be logged at DEBUG/TRACE. CI build output is publicly visible, so unobfuscated logging of cloud credentials or other secrets provided to CI runs is in scope, as are test resources like auth-keys.xml being printed or committed.

threats.name: Restricted Configuration instances resolving system properties
threats.description: org.apache.hadoop.conf.Configuration can restrict resolution of system properties and environment variables (setRestrictSystemProperties / setRestrictSystemPropertiesDefault), used by services to keep specific jobs/users from learning about the deployed system. If ${} or ${env.} references resolve within a restricted Configuration instance, that is a security vulnerability.

threats.name: Resource-exhaustion amplification from a single low-cost request
threats.description: General resource consumption issues are bugs, but rapid resource exhaustion triggered on HDFS and YARN services by remote requests from non-administrative callers is a special case: where a single low-cost request forces a disproportionate resource cost and degrades service for other users (an amplification attack), it is a vulnerability.

threats.name: Failures in Hadoop's own native code
threats.description: Anything triggering failures in Hadoop's own native code on supported operating systems is considered for CVEs: pointer/memory/stack issues, OS calls, process launch and cross-process IPC, and JNI binding. Issues in third-party native libraries such as libssl are out of scope unless Hadoop's invocation is at fault. Race conditions leading to privilege escalation within the security model are also CVEs.

threats.name: Java deserialization gadget chains reaching internal ObjectInputStream uses
threats.description: Java serialization persists some internal state (NodeManager recovery store, aggregated log index files in HDFS, ResourceManager configuration stores); the project catalogs these and wants notification if a gadget chain on service classpaths becomes attackable from untrusted network sources not guarded by HDFS or local filesystem permissions, or if a non-shaded org.apache.hadoop class can serve as a gadget in downstream deserialization attacks. Hadoop IPC itself uses Writable and protobuf, not Java serialization.

threats.name: Attacks on development and CI systems
threats.description: Development and CI are explicitly in scope: untrusted external-PR inputs (titles, comments, author metadata, code) reaching shell commands unsanitized; supply-chain subversion of non-ASF upstream dependencies; Maven plugins and third-party libraries executing code on developer/CI systems; IDE trust mechanisms (PRs adding code-execution files are rejected); and workflows granting unrestricted tokens to PR triggers.

threats.name: Attacks against the default insecure (non-Kerberos) mode
threats.description: In standalone configuration Hadoop performs no real authentication; anyone with network access has full access. This mode is insecure by design, intended only for network-isolated development/test hosts: "the unsecured cluster has no security" is not a vulnerability, and arbitrary data access against a non-Kerberos cluster is inherent in security being disabled.

threats.name: Job submission executing user-supplied code
threats.description: Submitting work to YARN or MapReduce executes the submitter's code as the submitter's identity: that is the product, not a vulnerability. A CVE report including a job-submission step on a kerberized cluster running the work as the submitting principal is immediately rejected, as is any attack against cloud storage using the credentials supplied to the VM/container the code runs in.

threats.name: Denial of service or resource exhaustion at scale from authenticated use
threats.description: A large Hadoop cluster exists to execute jobs at scale and authenticated users can exhaust resources; resource exhaustion and performance degradation from legitimate authenticated use are out of scope (except for the single-request amplification special case). Decompression bombs are bugs, not security issues; performance regressions are normal bugs.

threats.name: Attacks requiring compromise of trusted elements
threats.description: Vulnerabilities requiring compromise of trusted elements are outside the model: attacks needing operator edits to site configuration, malicious libraries on the classpath, malicious arguments to own command invocations, existing cluster/remote-store credentials or local disk access, a misconfigured or compromised OS, download and execution of external binaries, or capabilities the client already holds through its credentials (equivalent harm).

threats.name: Transitive CVEs in dependencies without a Hadoop reproducer
threats.description: Published CVEs in Hadoop dependencies are handled as public improvements in JIRA, not confidential security reports; raw scanner output without a reproducer against current trunk is rejected. CVEs reported against the shaded hadoop-client-* artifacts are almost always against bundled third-party code, remedied by dependency upgrades, not Hadoop CVEs. Bugs in third-party modules belong upstream. (Advance warning of a critical CVE in a bundled library is welcomed confidentially.)

trustBoundaries.name: Network perimeter trust boundary
trustBoundaries.description: The perimeter's job is to keep the cluster off the public internet; it does not authenticate callers. A report assuming a cluster directly exposed to the public internet is out of scope, and IPC endpoints need not resist the full scope of public-facing DoS attacks.

trustBoundaries.name: Authenticated service trust boundary
trustBoundaries.description: The boundary Hadoop defends: privilege escalation across an authenticated boundary within a Kerberos-secured cluster. Key IPC threats are unauthorized access (log and reject), privilege escalation (log and reject), and service vulnerability to malformed messages (logging and rejection is correct handling).

trustBoundaries.name: Infrastructure trust boundary
trustBoundaries.description: Administrators, DNS, the KDC, the OS, hardware/cloud providers, the site configuration, and the classpath are trusted; vulnerabilities requiring their compromise are outside the model's scope.

controls.name: Deploy in secure (Kerberos) mode for production
controls.description: Use a trusted Kerberos system to authenticate principals, issue services keytab credentials secured by OS file permissions, and authenticate all cluster users and inter-service communication via Kerberos; the insecure standalone mode is for firewalled development/test only.

controls.name: Service-level authorization and ACLs
controls.description: Restrict access to service endpoints to authorized callers via ACL site configuration (Service Level Authorization) and constrain proxy/superuser impersonation per the Superusers documentation.

controls.name: Delegation token lifecycle enforcement
controls.description: Delegation tokens have a limited lifespan of hours, can be cancelled (the issuing service must then reject them), and can be renewed before expiry; YARN distributes and renews tokens for applications so tasks need not hold Kerberos credentials.

controls.name: Keep clusters off the public internet
controls.description: Deploy behind a network perimeter with rules that keep the public internet out; Hadoop clusters (including transient cloud clusters) must not be deployed without network rules isolating them.

controls.name: Optional wire encryption and TLS validation
controls.description: Enable RPC privacy QOP and HDFS block-transfer encryption where confidentiality on the wire is needed; Hadoop services support TLS on service endpoints, and clients must validate certificates including hostname and the entire chain (certificate management itself is out of scope).

controls.name: HDFS transparent encryption for data at rest
controls.description: Persisting cluster-filesystem data encrypted requires configuring HDFS transparent encryption; temporary local data is secured (and where required encrypted) by the trusted OS.

controls.name: Store secrets in credential providers, not configuration files
controls.description: Secrets such as cloud credentials belong in JCEKS files or another credential provider service, not in shared XML configuration (where they become visible to all readers); application code must read secrets via Configuration.getPassword(). An administrator explicitly embedding secrets in configuration is their choice, not a vulnerability.

controls.name: Atomic creation and permission-setting of temporary files
controls.description: Code that creates temporary files and directories must create them and set their permissions atomically, never creating with permissive defaults and narrowing afterwards.

controls.name: Restrict log access and never log secrets
controls.description: Services must restrict access to logs (non-administrators must not read other principals' application logs or service logs); persistent secrets must never be logged and transient secrets not at INFO/WARN/ERROR; default log configurations should define size-limiting rollover, and services should provide specific logs for authentication failures and privilege rejections to assist central security logging.

controls.name: Restricted Configuration property resolution
controls.description: Configuration.setRestrictSystemProperties(true) (and the static default setter) prevents system-property and environment-variable references from resolving in configuration strings loaded for specific jobs/users, keeping deployment details from untrusted parties.

controls.name: Guarded internal deserialization and Java serialization filters
controls.description: Internal Java-serialization readers are cataloged; the ResourceManager ZK configuration store already uses an allow-listing ValidatingObjectInputStream, and deployments can restrict or block class deserialization via Java serialization filters (jdk.serialFilter, e.g. -Djdk.serialFilter=!*).

controls.name: CI and workflow hardening
controls.description: Treat all external-PR inputs as untrusted and never feed them to shell commands unsanitized; observe a cooldown before adopting new non-ASF dependencies; evaluate Maven plugins and compile-time libraries before adoption; pin GitHub Actions by commit SHA; forbid pull_request_target/workflow_run/issue_comment triggers that grant unrestricted tokens; follow GitHub secure-use guidelines and audit workflows with Zizmor; report CI-pipeline vulnerabilities to security@infra.apache.org.
